utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, I have already mentioned that I would like to address a few matters in relation to detection facilities. And with the help of the usher, I would like to put to you tab 5 of Exhibit 402.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You can get it from here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just want you to look at the page Camps Sorted By States where you also have the locations of the camps listed. First of all, in relation to the states, you have for Croatia, you have listed 2.404 detainees. Does this mean detention facilities in the RSK or does this also include camps run by the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers exclusively to the camps in Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to 802 detainees, you have listed here, "No information." Is that the same explanation that you gave yesterday, that some of the material was so scarce that you couldn't really say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The material was scarce, and we were dealing with detainees who were freed on a local level up until 1991, in the first stage, until official commissions, state commissions, had been set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the preparation of your testimony, did you look at camps in particular that are listed in the Croatia indictment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned during your testimony that a number of detainees were transferred from one camp to another. Would they be registered several times or just once?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the data I presented, a data -- when they were last in the camp. So that is to say from the camp they left. And they were recorded by the ICRC and through statements themselves saying that they had passed through several camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they would only show once in your files and that's the last camp they were in. I would like to turn first now to the -- to the camps in Montenegro, and I would like you to tell us, for the specific camps that I addressed, in addition to the number of detainees that are actually listed here, the time period of -- during which these detention camps existed, the kind of place it was, as far as you know, and whether you can say anything about the conditions in the camp, in particular about -- whether they were -- any abuse took place in these camps. The first camp I would like you to talk about is Morinje in Montenegro where you have listed the 346 detainees. What can you tell us in addition to that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that the office has, 346 detainees were listed as having been released from the Morinje camp. The camp in Morinje had the largest number of detainees between the 1st of October, 1991, and the middle of December 1991. According to the statements of the detainees themselves, the camp was within a military compound of warehouses where the conditions were extremely bad, without any sanitary conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the detainees in this camp came from which region? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detainees in the area of Crnogora, Montenegro, Morinje and Kumbor were from the Dubrovnik area in actual fact. So those camps catered to detainees from the Dubrovnik region. They were taken to those camps there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have next the camp Kumbor. When did it exist and was it a transit facility, and what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kumbor camp existed during that same time, between October and December 1991, and a small number of detainees we have listed with us was small because it was a transitory camp and detainees from Kumbor were later transferred to Morinje and other areas of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it a military facility? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a military facility or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now turn to Bosnia, and I would only like to address the camp Bileca. What can you tell us about this camp?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Bileca camp, 131 detainees were exchanged. The camp was set up between October and December 1991. That is to say before any conflicts had started in the region. And in Bileca, there was a great deal of abuse and mistreatment of detainees, and we have evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the previous camps in Montenegro, did you have any indication of abuse there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, in all the camps that we listed, there was physical abuse of detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to go to -- turn to Serbia, and you have -- and first of all, Stajicevo. What can you tell us about Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stajicevo was a camp to which detainees were brought mostly from the Vukovar area. And we have 661 detainees registered for Stajicevo. The camp had the largest number of detainees between the 18th of November, 1991, and the 21st of December, 1991. That particular camp was a facility that was on a factory farm, an agricultural concern, so quite inappropriate for accommodating human beings. And we evidenced the killing of war -- of war. For example, Branko Koch, Ivan Kunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people -- do you know how many people were killed there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least about ten people. But let me say specifically. Let me tell you something specifically about these two men that I mentioned by name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to say all I can talk about is about Branko Koch and Ivan Kunac, if you wish to hear some details concerning them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, unless there's a particular reason for hearing those details, I think there is so much evidence that we need to keep moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Stajicevo, I just want to know, was it also a transit facility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stajicevo was also a transit facility. Detainees from Stajicevo were later transferred to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica where detainees and prisoners were concentrated from other camps and prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Begejci, when did it exist, in which time period, and was it also a transit place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was also a transit camp. Most of the -- from the 1st of October, 1991, until the end of November 1991 was when the camp had the largest number of detainees. Once again, it was a farm managed by the JNA, and there were 55 detainees.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have actually the number in the list; Five hundred fifty-five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to which place were they transferred from there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there, they were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Zrenjanin, just one question: Was that also a transit place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, they would stay in Zrenjanin for a short period of time as well, and there was a place by Zrenjanin called Ecka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then now turning to Sid. Was that a military prison, and when did it exist?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prison in Sid was set up already on the 20th of July, 1991, and it existed until the 21st of January 1992. It was a military prison, and the detainees were transferred between the prison in the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, that is to say in the police station, to that military prison which was in a facility managed by the automobile school. And it was -- and there were 23 detainees listed in that particular prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned the number for Sremska Mitrovica, but can you tell us at which time periods detainees were detained there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detainees in Mitrovica were also held from November 1991, and after they were transferred from the Stajicevo and Begejci camps, which is where there were a large number of detainees, this penitentiary or house of correction in Serbia is where they were taken to, or rather, the last detainees were liberated from that particular facility in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say anything about the conditions? But only briefly.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were somewhat better than they were in Stajicevo and Begejci, but there were a large number of detainees in a small space. There were no hygienic, sanitary facilities, there was scant medical assistance, and it boiled down to detainees helping each other. That is to say if any of the detainees had any knowledge professionally in the field of medicine, they would help each other. And there were also some killings in the Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I would like to turn to Croatia, and first of all Knin. In which time period did the detention facilities in Knin exist, and what can you tell us about the conditions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Knin, there were 671 detainees that were evidenced between August 1991, up until November 1991. And the detainees were put up in the old hospital building and in the barracks. The conditions were listed as being exceptionally poor. The detainees were ill-treated and there was some killings as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dalj. What can you tell us about Dalj? When was it in operation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a camp in Dalj as well, yes, and it was located in the farm facilities, farm buildings, and in the police station itself. The camp was in existence from August 1991 to November 1991 with large numbers of detainees. There were 29 detainees, in fact, and some of the detainees were killed. And the names of the detainees are on a list in Annex I, paragraph 50, 51 and 55.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Vukovar, what can you tell us about the camp there? When did it exist? What was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the registrar would assist me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Vukovar, there were two main locations, although there were much more, but these two main ones had a large concentration of detainees, prisoners, and that was in the industrial facilities and industrial halls of Velepromet. That was one. And Komerc was the other, where at one point there were at least 723 individuals who were transferred from there to Stajicevo and Begejci in Serbia. And another portion was at Ovcara, also in the hall of the factory farm from which they were taken to the execution site at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what times did this detention facility operate?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those detention facilities were in existence -- or rather, from the 18th of November up until the end of November was when most of the detainees were held there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last one; Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Borovo Selo, we had a camp, and it was located in part in the school building, the sports hall of the school building, and the other half was in an industrial complex or, rather, the farm, the Lovas farm, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did these two camps operate; what time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those camps operated during that same period, that is to say from October -- and actually, the one in the sports hall itself was in existence already in August 1991. It had already been set up there then. And the Lovas farm facility came into being when large numbers of detainees came in from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The detention facilities in which no detainee was officially registered, would they show up in your list at all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Facilities did not show up on my list from which detainees were not freed on an exchange basis or were registered on the part of the ICRC. So this is the smallest number of camps, and the criteria was registration by the ICRC - the International Red Cross Committee - or the detainees being freed on an exchange basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that detainees were killed in these facilities. Do you know how many altogether?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say here and now, to give you a total number, but it increased as our investigations progressed. I know that about ten people at least were killed in Sremska Mitrovica, for instance, and we said that a large number of people were killed in the Borovo Selo camp. In the camps in Vukovar that we mentioned which were placed under Vukovar, the Borovo Komerc and Velepromet, many people were killed there whose bodies were later found in the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question: You mentioned that -- you mentioned the mistreatment in camps. Did you observe signs of this mistreatment on detainees that you personally met and dealt with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was engaged in the exchange of prisoners of war between 1993 -- from 1993 onwards, and I met a large number of people who had visible signs of injury when they were being exchanged. Let me also mention that all these detainees, the ones who were exchanged, after the exchange process, had to be treated medically where injuries were noticed, observed. And as I say, there is extensive medical documentation to bear that out. And I personally can testify to the fact that I saw some people who were physically abused, and this was quite obvious when they came up from the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now for you to cross-examine the witness. If there are matters which you want to challenge in his evidence, of course you're entitled to do so, but I must remind you that you must stick to his evidence, and we don't want a wide-ranging cross-examination about which he knows nothing. So you will be confined to asking about matters which he can deal with. You can have, if you require it, two and a quarter hours to cross-examine him. I hope you can perhaps do it more quickly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Mr. May, why these warnings, because if I ask a question that you consider to be irrelevant, you warn me of that very attentively. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grujic, you're a policeman, you have been a policeman since 1972; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the positions that you held in the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement that I gave, a detailed description is given of everything I did in the police, and I said that I was engaged in virtually all types of police work, ranging from a police clerk or a regular police officer right up to the level of inspector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, since when have you been a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my political affiliation is not of importance, but I can tell you that I am not a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a policeman, did you work in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. Milosevic. That is also contained in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you work in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1972 up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that in that period of time you were working in Osijek, you certainly know Branimir Glavas, Vladimir Seks, Vekic and others, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite know what you mean by knowing them. Yes, I know Vladimir Seks as a member of parliament. I also know Mr. Vladimir [sic] Glavas, who was head of the county of Osijek and Baranja. So I know Mr. Vekic too that you asked about, who was Minister of Internal Affairs in the ministry in which I was employed, so do I know them. So I can't say I really am familiar with them; I know of them. I may have had very superficial contacts with then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the activities they engaged in in that -- in the period of 1990 to 1992 while you were working in the Osijek police?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What activities?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The activities to expel in an organised manner, liquidate, dismiss Serbs from that entire area.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about those things because I don't know anything specific about those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't know, we'll move on. Tell me, once the HDZ came into power, who was the head of the state security in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Branko Budic, even before that, and he remained in that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you know, please, about the killing of the head of the Osijek SUP, Josip Reichl-Kir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Josip Reichl-Kir very well and I collaborated with him for many years, and I was present in the police building when we heard the news that he had been killed at a checkpoint between Tenja and Osijek. And an investigation was conducted, and it is still -- it still hasn't been completed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know nothing more about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a certain Gudelj was suspected as having committed that act who allegedly opened fire at that checkpoint. But the proceedings haven't been completed so I can't speak about it. I wasn't a direct participant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do know that the perpetrator was Gudelj, born in Tenja, near Osijek, and he is a fugitive in Australia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this to the case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant for this witness since this Reichl-Kir, head of the SUP in Osijek was killed because he opposed breaches of the law and the commission of crimes that were widespread at the time and also because, according to information I have, the witness, with Branimir Glavas and the mentioned Budic is linked to the organisation of the killing of this Josip Reichl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that is a very serious allegation indeed which you can put to the witness so that he may answer it. But how does it help us? Look, Mr. Milosevic, we are dealing with killings in the thousands, we're dealing with detained people in the thousands; how does it help us, even if it's right that this man was killed, what's the relevance of it? Even if you're right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If, Mr. May, you consider that not to be a relevant question for the witness, then let it be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I want you to say --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I want you to explain - it's your case - as to what the relevance is. Just explain it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it to be relevant because I have information that the perpetrator of this killing was this Gudelj, born in Tenja, and that the witness, together with Glavas and Budic, participated in organising the killing of the chief of police of Osijek who opposed violence and large-scale killings and liquidations of Serbs in that area at that time. So I assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Am I to understand -- do you say that that justified the detention and killings which occurred here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, a crime can never justify another crime, and you know that full well. This is just a question of the credibility of this witness, and I think that I am entitled to ask questions relating to the credibility of the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- regardless of what's testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask questions about the credibility, but what you need to think about is the connection between these allegations of wrongs done to the Serbs and the -- as alleged by you, and the facts that we have here, as put out by the Prosecution, as alleged by them, of killings and mass detention. And the question that you need to think about, because you're going to have to address us about it in due course, is what the relevance is, what the connection is. But we won't continue with this. You can certainly put that to the witness. You can ask him questions. In fact, I will. It's suggested, Mr. Grujic, that you were connected with this particular killing. Is there any truth in that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not true. Not a single allegation made by Mr. Milosevic linked to the killing of Mr. Kir. It is not true that I had anything to do with it, nor did I know anything about it until I heard that he was killed. And I must say that I -- this was a very painful event for me because he was a good friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was your position in the police station? What was your rank and position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time in those days, I was an operative officer covering the municipality of Osijek. And through that position, I collaborated very closely with Mr. Kir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move on, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Grujic. You have described here a very large number of victims of the civil war in Croatia, giving us numbers, sometimes even names, sometimes even individual locations and so on. So will you please answer this question for me: Who -- you're a policeman, and therefore you know very well what that entails. Who, when, where, under which circumstances killed those individuals for in such a testimony in this courtroom to -- for you to be able to present such data in testimony against me?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, where, and when, there are detailed information about that and there are witnesses, whereas my testimony was that of an expert Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness to find where the victims were found, what is the number of the victims, and not to say who, when, and where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those witnesses that you say that exist, and I will hold you to your word, do they have anything to do with Serbia and me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for him to answer. All he can give evidence about is what he investigated, the facts and figures which he came up with, the numbers and the like. Now, you can ask him about that and he can answer, but he can't answer about generalised questions about the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that is the crux of the matter, Mr. May. If you present here all the individual victims of the war and link them to this false indictment, then that is nonsensical. What has that got to do with Serbia and me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that is your case. Of course, that's the matter which we are having to decide. But at the moment we're dealing with this discrete part of the evidence. You can ask the witness about it, but you can't ask him about anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning, Mr. Grujic, at the beginning of your testimony yesterday, you spoke about bilateral meetings with representatives of an identical commission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there many such meetings?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very many, more than a hundred such meetings held in connection with these problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff yesterday insisted on the point that some of those meetings were attended not only by representatives of Yugoslavia and Croatia but also representatives of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or Republika Srpska. I haven't noted that down quite accurately. Maybe of both.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many such meetings were held at which these persons were included?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten or so. I can find you a list and the dates, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that won't be necessary. Tell me, please, did you understand the invitation and inclusion of those representatives in those meetings as a matter of goodwill prompted by the wish to solve the problem for which purpose the commissions were formed on both sides, or was this an indication, as being suggested by the other side, of the coordinating role of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt about the coordinating role. I can give you the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That is what you're claiming. You feel that that role was a coordinating one.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if I had arranged the release of prisoners from the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina who were imprisoned there with representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, then it is quite clear that this is coordination. Or if I arranged the discovery of a missing person in that area with that commission, then that is quite clear. Definitely that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Grujic. If you yourself say that a representative of the same commission from the Serbian Krajina or Republika Srpska is attending, then surely you arranged that with that representative and not with the representative of a country in which those prisoners were not being held. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am claiming again I arranged the release or discovery of a missing person specifically with Mr. Pavle Todorovic, for instance, to discover a person in Bosnia, specifically the pilot Peresin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't that the goodwill and assistance given by Todorovic who, as far as I can remember, was the Minister of Health, to assist you with the authorities of Republika Srpska to find the pilot? How else could he do that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate his goodwill, but we are talking here about competencies and about the real state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that competence later, but clear up one matter for me, please. Did I understand you correctly that all the detainees found in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were there from the time of the conflict with the JNA? That is the year 1991 and the beginning of 1992, when there was a large scale conflict between Croatian forces and the JNA on a broad front all over Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were detentions later on and detainees who were in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that there were captures carried out while the JNA did not exist, and they happened to be found in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have a list for that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give you the names straight away. For instance, Vanin Zlatko was captured in connection with armed conflict in the border area between Hungary and Yugoslavia. He was in a military investigating prison in Belgrade. After that, he was transferred to the territory of Krajina, that is Knin, and he was released there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. We didn't understand one another. My question was: Was anyone who was not captured in the conflict with the army, with the JNA, was he to be found as a detainee in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Was there any such person?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person was not captured by the JNA but by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. The police, probably on the border.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The border area with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there are other such examples, many such examples. And those persons were captured by the police, and they were in prisons in the territory of Yugoslavia from which they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they were imprisoned by the army or the police of Yugoslavia, I assume that they must have been imprisoned on the territory of Yugoslavia, or while the JNA were still present throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, they were captured by the JNA as prisoners of war. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose competence it was in those days nor is that the subject of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say only that those persons were in a facility that was in the territory of Yugoslavia, that is Serbia, that is Montenegro, that so many of them were detained there. As for competencies, I can't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Were they captured by the JNA during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only by the JNA but by paramilitary formations as well in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. So by paramilitary formations. And they found themselves in prisons in the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll clear that up fully eventually. So you're saying that Yugoslavia or, rather, its commission had a coordinating role in the exchanges. Tell me, this coordinating role or any role of the FRY commission, was this an expression of their willingness to cooperate or was something else behind it? Was it part of their wish to help deal with these humanitarian problems or was there something else behind it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, I said that I appreciated their cooperation designed to assist in the release and discovery of missing persons. But I also said that a dominant or, rather, coordinating role, to say the least, was played by the commission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as compared to the commission from Republika Srpska and the commission that existed in the occupied parts of Croatia, that is the commission of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Grujic. Tell me, now, your commission, the commission that you headed for detainees and missing persons, did it engage in identical activities and often advocated the interests of the commission of Croats in the -- from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have cooperation with commissions from Bosnia, both with the commission, the Bosniak commission, and also the commission of the then Herceg-Bosna. And that particular cooperation was actually at a level of cooperation, that's true, but we never acted in the sense of the fact that the Republic of Croatia could do something linked to detainees in the territory of Bosnia while I was on the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Grujic. Now, do you know about a letter that you yourself signed as president of the Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons in which you addressed the commission for exchange in Sarajevo presided over by Bulajic, a man whose name was Bulajic, on the 28th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what all this is about. I entered into a great deal of correspondence with representatives of various commissions; the commission of the RSK, with Yugoslavia, the federations commission, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in point 1 of that letter, "On the list there are a large number of persons for which the Republic of Croatia did not make any requests, 108. With respect to these people, we sought the opinion of the HVO commission from Herceg-Bosna." So what this means is you're seeking confirmation and opinions in order to continue to act. So you're coordinating that affair, and you say: "After that, we'll be able to determine our position with respect to the status of those persons," and so on and so forth, "and inform you thereof." So that is your own letter, dated the 28th of June in which undoubtedly you are asking for confirmation and the opinions of the commission of Herceg-Bosna in order for you to be able to pursue matters related to their exchange. Are you challenging that, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, Mr. Grujic. The witness should see the letter. He can't possibly remember it. He should have the opportunity of looking at it and commenting on it. So would you give it to the usher, please, if you want him to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, are you challenging the contents of the letter?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to have a look at it first to be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's indulgence, may I -- well, if we have to discuss this particular portion, it would be a good idea for the whole letter to be read out, because the portion that Mr. Milosevic quoted has been pulled out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the whole of point 1.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear that I did send this letter, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will you just tell us what it is, please, what the letter is about, and then you can deal with the particular area that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Milosevic is asking you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it's about: The president of the commission, at negotiations in Novska of the Republika Srpska handed over a list of persons in prisons on the territory of Bosnia, and that particular list, when we analysed it, we ascertained that on the list were persons who were not the subject of interest of the Republic of Croatia, and that persons we were interested in were not on the list of detainees. And it was precisely for that reason that I wrote that particular letter to Mr. Bulajic, bringing his attention to those facts. And in the letter, I stipulate what Mr. Milosevic just read out, that I would send the list to the commission of Herceg-Bosna or, rather, the HVO, for them to take a look at it and to see if anybody on their list was on this other list so that we can then take further steps to agree upon what we were going to do. That meant that if the persons were on the list that the Republic of Croatia had no interest in, which I state here quite specifically, that meant that they could not discuss those persons but would be sent on to the Herceg-Bosna commission. The fact that I coordinated, or rather, not coordinated but managed these affairs for Herceg-Bosna, I would never have written this letter to Mr. Bulajic, nor would I have referred to him to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, as far as I recall, and you have the text in front of you, you say in the letter that you're going to take steps in that regard only once you have had consultations and received confirmation and the opinions of the HVO from Herceg-Bosna. So you can read out the whole of point 1 out loud. Please go ahead, read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would read the whole letter, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I don't have time to read through all the letters in full.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you cannot pull something out of context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not out of context. It is the whole of point 1, that first paragraph. And you say when you received confirmation and their opinions - so they are to give their confirmation and opinions - for you to be able to take a decision in the matter. So that is point 1. And I'd like to have that tendered into evidence, please, and the Court can ascertain for itself what the letter says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could hand it in and it could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what's bad in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no. Let's get an exhibit number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Defence Exhibit 107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Grujic, please, is there anything bad in the fact that the commission of the RSY for exchanges, which sometimes advocated the commissions -- which sometimes represented the RS and RSK commission positions when your commission did the same, it represented the interests of Herceg-Bosna. Is there anything bad in that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of representing anybody's interests. What all this is about is how far it was able to influence the other commissions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I assume, Mr. Grujic, that in those commissions everybody wanted to wield as much influence as possible to have as many people exchanged as possible and to alleviate the consequences of that war. To help people. I assume that that's what the commissions wanted and that they all worked in similar fashion to achieve that end. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ask me your question. I don't know what you mean, what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't all the commissions, each on its own side, endeavour to help people, ultimately, and to cooperate with the opposite side and perform its job, do its duty?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that my own commission did wish to assist people, but I can't speak on behalf of the other commissions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that you replaced as president of the commission Josip Kardum? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you now is this: Confirmation of this practice of your commission, is it contained in points 2 and 3 that were sent out by your commission to the Commission for Exchange of Prisoners in Banja Luka? And you state that if any individual requested by your commission should be released within the scope of another exchange process, you would consider their duties done vis-a-vis you. So that is the letter to the Commission for Prisoner Exchange, and it says: "Persons detained by the Republic of Croatia that we would like to see exchanged," what the Republic of Croatia is requesting, and then it says at the end here: "We consider that exchanges of this kind should be an addition to the Geneva agreements and Budapest agreements. And we stress that if the person we request be released should be released in another operation, we will consider that you have done your duty towards us, and the same principle must be applied on both sides." Does this also indicate that there was coordination along those lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here it is. Have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if we proceed at this pace, then our time will be up very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to read through the document you've just given me, and what I've read through here indicates that the Croatia commission sent a letter to the Commission for Prisoner Exchange in Banja Luka and expresses their satisfaction at what they have offered by way of exchange and states that the information that the commission has indicates that prisoners will not be released from other camps in Bosnia, which was something agreed upon in Geneva. But they propose that the following detainees be exchanged, and then we have a list of the detainees in question, and I don't see anything to take issue with there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your letter?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed by Josip Kardum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of your commission?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I see nothing to take issue with there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, whether there is or not, let's leave that alone. But all I'm asking you is, is that your letter?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain this to me then, please, and you can hand over the letter to Mr. May if you are inclined to do so, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 108.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you mentioned a moment ago that some people -- you mentioned one particular man who was in Belgrade and then came -- found himself in Knin. We'll get to that later. But could you explain, please, how it was that the Serbs from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina happened to be -- to find themselves in camps on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, for example?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be more specific and tell me what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you have occasion to see that Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example, were in camps of the Republic of Croatia? How did that come about? How did they happen to turn up in camps in Croatia, a Serb from Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were different possibilities. So tell me what you mean specifically for me to be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that on the list of detained Serbs put up for an exchange which you attached to your letter, the Commission for Prisoner Exchange on the 2nd of July, 1993, that there was a number of Serb detainees from the BH territory? Do you know about that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where those people were taken prisoner. They could have had nationality or residence in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Yugoslavia, but where they were actually taken into custody, taken prisoner, I can't say because I don't know. So if they were to be found in camps, they might have been captured somewhere in connection with the armed conflict. So it was my job to have these people exchanged or released. Now, under which circumstances they had come to be in prison and in the camps in the first place, I don't know nor could I have known, nor could I speak about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, I'm not going to hand you the list then because you do not dispute the fact that there were Bosnia-Herzegovina citizens who were in Croatian camps.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to see what you're talking about, what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, here you have, then, a list of prisoners that were incorporated into the exchange, prisoners in Croatia, and it was the 2nd of July, 1993, an attachment, a letter written by you and a list by you. You can see where the people were captured. Take a look at it, please, if you would.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From this list I don't see where they were captured nor what -- the national of which country. It just lists the names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, Mr. Grujic, and hurry up. Is it true that in the negotiations that you held during the exchange with representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the Republika Srpska, representatives of the FRY did not take part, nor did they authorise anybody to negotiate on their behalf? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What did you say? You asked whether they took part?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did the representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia take part or authorise anybody to take part in the negotiations on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recall, for example, in Bocac, there were representatives -- Bocac is in Bosnia, by the way, representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were there when negotiations, talks, took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. I'll quote another letter of the 2nd of July, 1993, point 3, and I'll leave out parts that are irrelevant for what I am claiming. I'm saying they did not; you say they did. It says, I quote: "In view of that as well as the fact that in contact so far representatives of the commission from Belgrade did not take part nor did they authorise anyone to negotiate on their behalf. We take the liberty Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to emphasise the following," and then you list various things. All this because representatives of Belgrade did not take part, nor did they authorise anyone to negotiate on their behalf, and you're claiming the opposite. And at the end, in point 5, it says: "Also in view of the fact that we don't know who exactly needs to be received in Novska or Livno, we propose that the exchange with respect to persons held in the Republic of Croatia, or rather, which the Republic of Croatia has been searching for, we say that we do not mind if an exchange be carried out in Livno of the prisoners agreed on between your commission and the commission of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." So here we see this other matter testifying to your coordinating role on behalf of Herceg-Bosna. The first point is on page 1 of this letter, and the second point is on page 2. So I'll give you the letter as a whole so that you can see for yourself that at the beginning it says, I quote: "That in view of the fact that representatives of the commission from Belgrade did not participate nor did they authorise anyone to negotiate on their behalf," end of quote. That is one point. And the second point has to do with the fact that you were organising an exchange in Livno in Herceg-Bosna, and again this was signed by your predecessor, Josip Kardum. Just look at it, please, and then we can move on. And as there is a transcript, there is no doubt as to my having quoted correctly. Mr. Grujic, is it quite clear that your commission, the commission of the Republic of Croatia, was involved in the exchange of prisoners in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is clear, because we had a large number of detainees that were detained in camps in the territory of Bosnia, and there is no dispute over that. So we were looking for possibilities for them to be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But my specific point is is there any dispute that your commission negotiated on behalf of the commission of Herceg-Bosna, that is a commission of the Croatian Community in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of negotiating on their behalf but rather their assistance to receive detainees in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, I would not insist on this at all if Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff had not insisted on this practice in your communications with a commission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which she probably considers to be something negative. So I'm trying to strike at least some balance and to avoid the impression that whatever is happening in Yugoslavia is negative. So from this letter you see that your commission organising an exchange in Livno, which is in Herceg-Bosna; right? And these are prisoners from Herceg-Bosna, and on other hand, prisoners of the Muslim federation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it has to be known that it was not possible to carry out an exchange in areas between Republika Srpska and the Republic of Croatia because of war operations. You know that there was the corridor along the Sava River, and it was impossible. An exchange of prisoners could only be done in the southern part where detainees from Republika Srpska were transferred to that area and citizens of the Republic of Croatia were then transported to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, please don't say these things, because after you there will be a witness who will be talking about the time of the war conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So she will be coming immediately after you. So if we're talking about the since July, 1993, that was the period of conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any dispute that representatives of the Croatian army were in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there's no dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you try to move on, what are you going to do with this letter? Would you like to exhibit it, or shall we return it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I would like it to be exhibited, because it fully denies what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was trying to allege about the Yugoslav side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that your commission frequently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Wait a moment. Before we go on, the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Defence Exhibit 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just give me a brief yes or no answer, please. That will suffice. I'm just asking you, is it true that your commission, in spite of agreements reached, concealed prisoners, especially members of the JNA that should have been exchanged? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have to be more specific. What do you mean did the commission hide them? How can the commission conceal them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were silent about their existence, did not reveal information about them, concealed their existence.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you a very brief answer, Mr. Milosevic. All detainees in the Republic of Croatia during my term of office were certainly registered by the International Committee for the Red Cross. And this means that they could exchange family messages with members of their family regardless of where the family was, which means that their family members knew that they were in prison. Therefore, that is the mechanism whereby we obtained information about some prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that your commission, on the 22nd and 23rd of July, 1992 negotiated with the Commission for Exchange of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Subotica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is a report about that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it. You have seen how long I have held this position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know, Mr. Grujic, that on your list a large number of JNA members were missing even though representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross and some released members of the JNA claimed that in camps in Croatia there were a large number of prisoners, members of the JNA? I'm saying this to provide evidence or to corroborate my claim that the number of prisoners was minimised and facts were concealed about existence of these prisoners, those the International Red Cross was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is possible. All prisoners registered by the International Committee of the Red Cross were registered. And today we have reports from the International Committee of the Red Cross saying that in the territory of the Republic of Croatia those prisoners that were registered are still not being held, whereas in other parts of the former Yugoslavia there were still such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a letter here, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Ministry of Defence, the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners, a letter addressed to the 1st Krajina Corps, in which it says: "We enclose a list of captured members of the army of Yugoslavia and civilians handed to us by the Croatian government delegation during talks in Subotica on the 22nd and 23rd of July, 1992. The Croatian side claims that the list is final and complete. However, after analysing that list, we have come to the conclusion that there are large numbers of prisoners, members of the army and civilians, that we are searching that they are not, rather, they are not on this list. Among them, there are many who have been seen by the International Committee of the Red Cross, by released persons, and family members." Does this tell you anything, Mr. Grujic, or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see that letter, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give it to you a little later. Let me just address another point. You claimed yesterday that Tole Zarko, a soldier, was first -- of the Croatian army was first held in Serbia and then moved to Knin.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned Tole Zarko in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about a person captured over there and then transferred to Knin.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not Mr. Tole Zarko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who is it, then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the lists and then I'll give you the names. But it is certainly not Mr. Tole Zarko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this letter by General Radinovic, it says that this citizen of yours was arrested in the territory of FRY. He was not engaged in any combat operations. He had on him a forged passport with which he had come to the Federal Republic from the Czech Republic, that he spent some time in prison as an ordinary criminal and not as a prisoner of war, and that he was handed over to the Republic of Serbian Krajina because the authorities there were looking for him because of war crimes committed in Slunj where Tole was born. And this is what it says in this letter by General Radinovic: "In connection with the captured member of the Croatian army, soldier Tole Zarko, and his escort, we wish to inform you that they are in the prison at Knin and under the authority of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Please contact the responsible authorities in Knin regarding the possible exchange of Tole Zarko and his escort." If you're interested, you can look at this letter.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to see the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please read the last passage, which refers to the missing names on your list, and then this particular passage regarding this particular individual.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can comment on this letter. So the letter is being sent by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Ministry of Defence, to the 1st Krajina Corps, which means to Bosnia, to the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners. So the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is writing to the Krajina Corps. In the letter, they say that they have information that a certain Tole Zarko was arrested, that we did not mention at all here during my testimony, and that this same person is under the authority of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and they are advising us to have further contacts regarding exchange. That is, the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners is asking the 1st Krajina Corps to take steps for the exchange. And also, they say that they are providing a list of prisoners handed over by the commission for Croatia. Therefore, at all negotiations the current list of prisoners or detainees were exchanged -- were exchanged for those detainees to be exchanged, which doesn't mean that all the detainees needed to be on those lists. All registered detainees would normally appear on those lists. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But here they say that the Ministry of Defence analysed the list provided, and on the basis of their information, without any grounds, they claim there should be more names. We also analysed lists and claimed that a detainee may have been here or there. So that was one of the ways of finding detainees. But from this letter, we see absolutely no grounds to claim that except that they had analysed the list. And the other grounds is -- and another point is that this is a relationship between Yugoslavia and Bosnia. This letter confirms the existence of that relationship that we mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want that to be exhibited, this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, it may be convenient to adjourn now. Mr. Grujic, could you be back, please, in twenty minutes to conclude your evidence. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it occurs to me it may be sensible to discuss the Vukovar witnesses, Rule 92 bis, after this witness. We ought to do something of that this week , before we call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's also an issue that should be dealt with today in view of the fact that we have a three-day break. That concerns the recent filings about Ambassador Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't had those yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They're in the system, and Your Honour may recollect that Mr. Nice mentioned it yesterday in open session with a date which the Prosecution had an interest in securing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one additional matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have actually scheduled two witnesses where decisions are outstanding for next week. That is the witness Baca, which we want as a replacement for Franic, and also the witness Rousseau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We can deal with Rousseau. Baca I'm not so sure about. But anyway, let's adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, as we have just observed that it is not contentious that Croatian armed forces were on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you happen to know how many Serb prisoners, detainees who were held in Odzak, that is to say on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were transferred after July 1992 to Croatia and put up in camps throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. I can't answer that question. I don't have that information. I did say earlier on that I do not have facts and figures of that kind, where people were captured and taken prisoner. All I can testify about is where people were released and when they were released from prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. But now let's look at some figures, the figures you yourself gave us. But before we come to that, let me just remind you of the following: At a meeting of the Croatian parliament on the 15th of January, 1996, the late president, Franjo Tudjman, presented some information to the fact that there were 10.668 persons killed and 2.215 missing persons. Later on, those figures were adjusted so that the total of missing and killed persons was somewhat lower, or rather, the total of persons killed was increased and the persons missing, the number was reduced somewhat. So the figure that was arrived at was a percentage, actually. The percentage of persons killed and missing with respect to the number of inhabitants of Croatian ethnicity was 0.35 per cent. I assume you will recall that, and you have that figure.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it is justified to express this in percentages and to add up apples and pears. You can't put persons who were missing and persons who were killed into one category. I don't think that's the right way to go about it. But as to figures, the figures of those missing and those killed changed depending on the period, and the number of missing persons that were actually found, the number of graves located, so that the time distance and time factor is very important linked up to these figures. As to the figures that I presented here during my testimony, I stand by them. I stand by each and every number I uttered, because there is always a name and a surname, an individual behind a number, and personal ID and data, whether we are referring to missing persons or persons killed. So this is the information that my office has at its disposal, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But at all events, Mr. Grujic, if we leave aside the number of persons missing and not link it up and add it to the number of persons killed, then the percentage is lower than that 0.35 per cent that I quoted a moment ago. But tell me this, please. Let's clear up one matter first of all: Of the number of persons killed, the figure that you testify about, which is 11.800-odd -- and just help me what the exact figure was. 11.800 and how many? 11.834. I have it here, yes, of persons killed. So that is the total number of Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is the total number of persons killed regardless of their ethnic affiliation, excluding people who lost their lives after 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, within the number of persons killed, how many of them were members of the Croatian armed forces, the Croatian National Guards Corps, and the HVO who were killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not talking about individuals here and members of the HVO, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we're talking about, and I'm sure that is why your information is different, the facts and figures here referred to the territory of the Republic of Croatia exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you claiming that among this figure of 11.800-odd persons we do not have any members of the Croatian armed forces who were killed on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. That's what I'm claiming. Any possible -- there could be a slight mistake, but I doubt that you will be able to actually find a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you list members who were killed of the regular Croatian army on the territory of Herzegovina or members of the Croatian National Guard Corps killed on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Where are they listed? How are they registered? So members of the Croatian armed forces who were killed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if they are not included in that figure, where are they included?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I explained how these lists and these registers came into being, I said that it was the ministries, that they did it, and there was the Ministry of Defenders and that the Ministry of Defenders will have information and lists of all those killed who were members of the armed forces. And following on from that logic, in undertaking this analysis, we presented data which referred exclusively to the territory of the Republic of Croatia. So anything about those killed on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would not have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you say that this percentage, which is below 0.35 per cent --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to delve into percentages. I didn't give percentages, nor did I calculate this in percentages, and I think that to be the wrong approach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether it's the wrong approach or not, what I'm asking you is do you know that the percentage of Serbs killed is far greater, several times greater, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What do you mean? What do you mean, and what is the relevance? All this witness is dealing with is the number of killed who he has recorded. The fact that you've got some other figure for some other group is irrelevant. What's the relevance of it as far as this witness's evidence is concerned, even if you're right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question is as follows, Mr. May. As -- well, let me explain, give a brief explanation before I go on to ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, according to the census of Croatia in 1991, the lists made in Croatia then, Croatia had 4.774.265 inhabitants, according to the 1991 population census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all irrelevant, but I will ask Mr. Grujic this: In the figures which you gave, do you record Serbs who were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are in the records, Serbs, ethnic Serbs in the Republic of Croatia. What I can tell you is that on that list we have recorded the following, as we're dealing with figures: 6.790 persons were ethnic Croats, and 298 persons were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the number of persons killed, Mr. Grujic? Well, you say several hundred ethnic Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the ones that we have recorded as having been killed. These are the official records of the Republic of Croatia, and in those records, for understandable reasons because we don't have the figures, we have not recorded members of the paramilitary units that were killed and buried previously. So they were not recorded because we don't have information of that kind within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you -- have you ever heard of Veritas? It's an institution dealing with crimes against humanity and Serb victims in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, that is a non-governmental agency; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So instead of this figure that you have, some 200-odd or 300 Serbs killed, do you know that their records, which have been verified, that the figure there is 6.744, in fact, persons killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is that for? For paramilitaries and the like killed in Serbia -- killed in Croatia? Is that what that figure includes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about this: Mr. May, it seems to be that there's some confusion here, as you understand it. Mr. Grujic is the director of an institution dealing with persons killed, missing, expelled, or rather, the victims of war in Croatia. I am talking about the -- about Serbs who were Croatian nationals, and I'm asking Mr. Grujic why you don't deal with Serbs who were Croatian nationals and expelled, missing, or killed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we do deal with that too. We do deal with ethnic Serbs, and that can be seen from the list of missing persons that I submitted. So all those who were registered with the office, all the ethnic Serbs, the exhumed bodies that were identified have been recorded and are on the list Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of persons killed. But when you speak about the Veritas figures and you said that was 6.700-odd, I don't wish to comment on that specifically. I have reports by them which speak of lower figures. But regardless of that, what I can tell you is this: There are certain questionable things and uncertitudes on that list, for example. People who died a natural death are also on those lists. For example Luka Andzelic, Basta Andja, two cases in point. And then we have persons who are still living. For example, Ljubica Batula, Drago Borojevic, Djuro Borojevic and persons who were reported missing in Kosovo, such as Djuro Barac in Pristina, Nikola Begovic in Orahovac, persons who went missing in the BiH territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You needn't enumerate.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. So persons missing in the BiH territory, such as Igor Alisic [phoen], Dusko Babic, Srdjan Mitrovic at Pale. Therefore it is because of these shortcomings that list is not relevant and pertinent. But I can answer your question and say yes, I do deal with ethnic Serbs, and we have just completed a list on the territory of Serbia and Montenegro, persons who went missing there. And we initiated and launched this drive in Croatia using Croatian criteria, and this kind of list was compiled and completed in Bosnia too. So yes, we do deal, and very seriously, with Serb -- ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. According to the method and way in which you do this, as far as I can gather, Mr. Grujic, you list the Serbs killed, and there are several hundred of those on your list, whereas Veritas, the figure Veritas gives us is several thousands. Do you note a drastic difference between those two figures or are you claiming that your figures are the correct ones?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that my figures are the correct ones and there is a difference. The list of Veritas is called persons killed, missing, and so on. It entails all the categories. So apart from the shortcomings I've already mentioned, there is another very serious shortcoming: The difference in figures and numbers exists because the information that I presented refers to facts and figures dating from 1991 up to 1995.
