utterances.text: What about 3? The Trial Chamber is concerned about the restriction of the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is, of course, a -- two things about that: First of all, it matches the relief granted in the other witness to whom reference is obliquely made and of whom the Chamber will have a recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And upheld by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think so, yes, but I'm not sure about that. The -- it's a condition, part of the conditioned consent of the relevant authority. The third point is that there will, of course, be, if you so decide, lawyers present on behalf of that party who will be able to respond on the spot, or effectively on the spot, to any applications to go outside the prima facie restrictions of that condition. It's not something about which we can do any more at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if we make the order at the moment in the terms asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- but with leave to apply to go outside it, that would leave it open to the accused to ask questions outside it, with leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With leave, and of course, with -- well, if the condition's been granted in those terms, the witness is prima facie authorised to say nothing. The unlocking -- I don't know what his immediate and personal response might be. His enthusiasm might be contrary to the attitude of those imposing the restriction, I suspect, but that's a problem we regularly have to deal with with this type of evidence. But the advantage, of course, of having representatives of the other body here is that those representatives can be spoken to and it may be that they'll then be in a position to modify the condition upon which the giving of evidence has been predicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it is a condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is a condition as it stands at the moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when we attempted to interpret Rule 70 in a more liberal manner, we were told by the Appeals Chamber we had to apply it strictly, as I recollect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the position, yes. I express no views one way or another personally, it's not for me to do so. But I have to operate within it and my guiding principle has always been to make sure that whatever other conditions may be attached that I can respectably and properly present, as I do these, there should be no infringement to the right to a public trial, and we've made great progress there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will -- we will make the order as asked. We think it right. This is an important witness. There are reasons why -- good reasons as to why the witness hasn't appeared on the witness list before, namely that he has not been available. Therefore, we think it right to add his name to it. We, having regard to the interpretation which was given to Rule 70 by the -- strict interpretation by the Appeals Chamber, we will grant the relief asked in terms of the restriction on questioning, and the representative of the government being present, we will grant the relief asked. However, we do not think it right, in the circumstances of his being an important witness, to spring him upon the trial and upon the accused within a week. The accused should have more time to prepare, because preparation may include research with his associates. He should have more than a week. So we'll say that he's not to be called next week but later in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. We'll list him probably towards the end of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move from dealing with his evidence to the other two who appear on the list about whom there are applications, and we can perhaps deal with them together. There's Ms. Zana Baca, if I've pronounced her name right. She is a specialist on war-related damage, and the notion is that she deals with protected -- the damage to protected monuments of the old town. Dubrovnik I should say, yes, and she replaces another witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is exactly -- actually, exactly the same subject as the other witness who is not available, and she will also deal with the issues of protection raised by Judge Robinson. You know, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the issue of protection. And is there any reason why she shouldn't be, if you put her statement in, dealt with under Rule 92 bis? Well, that's for you to consider.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes we'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you care to deal with her in that way. And while you're on your feet, Mr. Rousseau is the ECMM monitor. You ask for his statement to be admitted. It doesn't relate to the accused directly. You want certain paragraphs to be dealt with live, paragraphs 5 to 7, as far as I can see. It's 6, but I think 5 for the sense. 1, 2, 4, and 8 to 11 Rule 92 bis, and the rest would not be admitted. Yes. Any point about either of those two, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. No we had no observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, anything about those two?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This doesn't matter. But could you please tell me, instead of which witness? I understood Mrs. Retzlaff to say that this witness would be testifying instead of another witness that's already on the list. So I can strike that particular witness off my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You should know that. According to the papers we have in front it, it is to replace Mr. Zvonimir Franic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he won't be testifying; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Very well. We'll admit those statements as asked. We will consider Ms. Baca's under Rule 92 bis when it's ready. We will admit her evidence, taking off Mr. Franic from the list. It may be more convenient to spend the rest of the session dealing with Rule 92 bis rather than embarking on the next witness. The witnesses who I signalled that we would deal with were those dealing with Vukovar, and I had seven, beginning with C-006, C-171, 1126, 1149, 1164, and 1165. Beginning with C-006, I have a note that this looks to have been a Dokmanovic witness and therefore I am inquiring as to why it wasn't appropriate to serve that particular transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, to -- I don't think that he was a Dokmanovic witness. I think he was not called. According to my information, he was not called in the Dokmanovic case, and I can't actually see the reason why he was not called, but he was not called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you check that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's quite possible that I have my notes wrong on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. McKeon, whom you know already from this trial, has checked the data, and he informed me that this person was not called in the Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, very well. He deals with events at Ovcara when the detainees were in the hangar, as far as I could see, and he let some of them out. He's one witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was actually present in Velepromet. He was present in the barracks where the people were taken first, and he made a lot of observation in relation to Sljivancanin, Vujovic, and Vujanic, the person in charge. Also at Ovcara he saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since one of the issues that has been raised by the accused is the role of the JNA in the Vukovar incident, it may be that this is a witness who should be called for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would agree to this, because he seems to be quite important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We referred to this witness in our schedule as part of our filing to the Trial Chamber, because the description of his evidence in the Prosecution summary we didn't think was entirely accurate, and so we make an observation at paragraph 19 that this could not necessarily be considered as cumulative evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are other considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I make that so the Trial Chamber is alert to the perhaps extra matters that this witness dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But we have in mind to admit with cross-examination. Mr. Milosevic, anything you want to say about that particular witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what witness we're talking about anyway. I haven't got this in my documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You haven't got it. C-006. He's a Vukovar witness, as these all are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That doesn't mean -- tell me anything. I haven't got a review of the witnesses, their names, the contents of their testimony, and I didn't know that this would be discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I did say last week that we would be discussing this issue, and I read out more than once the list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit this witness with cross-examination. In terms of the numbers, I think the next one which would come is 1071. This is the widow, if I have it right, of a man who was arrested by the JNA, taken from the football field, and it's alleged subsequently shot. And really, the evidence, a great deal of it, is taken up with her search, fairly harrowing search, for her husband, and unsuccessful. You would ask that this be admitted without cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is she a protected witness? What circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So her name is Zorica Brajdic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And is a crime-base witness for Lovas farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Murdered in the field. You know, the minefield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's not my note. My note is it's, unless we're at cross-purposes about the field, a man who was taken from -- she's the widow of a man taken from the football field and subsequently shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. He was murdered in a field. He was taken away from Vukovar, that's correct, but the crime as such occurred in Lovas. So the crime base is Lovas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Lovas field, not the minefield.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it was the field, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But he was shot. Yes, Mr. Kay, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The observations we have about this is that it's cumulative in relation to Vukovar, but there's the additional features within her evidence where she deals with an area called Rupe near Olajnica and the transport of herself and her daughters to Brsadin. It's additional matters within the statement which then fall into evidence, although not strictly speaking being part of a specific allegation within the indictment. It's at tab 5 in the statements, this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will reserve on this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just let me explain in relation to this one, and also that applies equally for number C-1126. What we want to say is that what these witnesses say is corroborative in relation to pattern of ethnic cleansing that occurred in regions and of -- about which other witnesses have talked about, and so far it is cumulative. In addition to that, admittance of written statements according to 92 bis does not necessarily afford a cumulative nature of the evidence. That's just what I would like to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next one will be 1126. Dealing with a particular form of evidence, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just mentioned this case where we also have the witness speaking about a different village, but what she actually is testifying to will be the pattern of ethnic cleansing, and so far the same that applies to 1071 would apply here. That is all I would have to add to this witness. She speaks about a different village not yet addressed. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The difficulty with this witness is, of course, that a witness expected to testify viva voce is the express source of the cumulative evidence. The Prosecution identify [redacted], and so it's difficult to deal with the cumulative nature of it because of that difficulty, although within the Rules that is permitted, witnesses who will testify or have testified being the source of the cumulative nature of the evidence. The Prosecution have already made a submission about the fresh evidence being cumulative of ethnic cleansing generally, because the point is made by us in our schedule that the witness dealing with Opatovac and the JNA entry into Opatovac is fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit, but with cross-examination. Yes. Let's try and do another one. 11 -- 1164 and 1165. 1164 deals with the shelling of Vukovar. The witness was arrested in September and taken to Begejci camp. 1165 is the forensic pathologist who simply testifies about the bodies found at Ovcara, a matter about which there has been no dispute, as I recollect, no mention of the JNA. Perhaps you could help us with those two, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Is there anything further we should consider?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the pathologist, he actually made observation in relation to the parts of the bodies and actually, the witness, Dr. Strinovic, who is supposed to testify next week, will deal with this aspect. So that is clearly corroborative. So I think that shouldn't be a problem, because Mr. -- Dr. Strinovic is actually the head -- the medical -- the Croatian medical examiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the other one, I think I summed it up rightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And actually, the additional underlying other evidence is the evidence of Mr. Grujic, who referred to the camp where the witness had actually been detained in. So for both, we would request without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I deal with tab 38, which is 1164 first, [redacted]. Cumulative in respect of Vukovar but with reference to the JNA and the White Eagles, an eyewitness account of shelling in July 1991 in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will reserve that one. But the next one is the pathologist. What reason is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We just mentioned it was a distinct category of being a pathologist but with nothing extra to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, we're going to reserve on the first witness, so we won't ask you to consider that. The pathologist, is there anything you want to say about that, why we shouldn't admit the pathologist's evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of admission of evidence. I just insist on my right to cross-examine each and every witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, in that case, we can see no good reason to cross-examine. There's been no dispute that these people were shot. There will be other evidence about it. We shall admit it under Rule 92 bis. It falls within all the categories for admission and none for cross-examination. So 1165. Perhaps Prosecution would produce that at our next sitting with the necessary attachments and we can exhibit it. Well, while we're waiting for something, apparently the registrar has a matter to deal with it, have you got the statement? Let's exhibit it now. C-1164.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have the 92 bis form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. We are ahead of ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We cannot admit it, we simply indicate that we will Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't facilitate the process without having you confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness who was to start today, not having even started and there being a four, five-day break and that witness no doubt returning home in the meanwhile, I can't guarantee that we'll stick to her as the next witness. It may be inconvenient for her and more convenient to slightly re-order the witnesses for next week. We will send a letter as soon as we know the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Provided the accused has reasonable notice of any change --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- so he can prepare properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of March, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
